title: Plans and the weather
summary: The future is usually the present tense with a time word (Morgen werk ik). gaan + infinitive: a plan, or something about to happen. zullen + infinitive: a promise, a guess (zal wel), a forecast. The infinitive goes last.
explain:
Dutch grammar books call `zullen` + infinitive the future tense (*de toekomende tijd*), but in real life that is not the usual way to talk about later. There are three ways, and the most common one is the simplest: the present tense.

### 1. The present tense with a time word

When a time word or the situation makes clear that it is about later, the present tense is enough. This is what people say most of the time.

> Morgen regent het de hele dag. — Tomorrow it will rain all day.
> Vanavond blijf ik thuis. — I am staying at home this evening.
> Over twee dagen begint de vakantie. — The holiday starts in two days.

Time words you will need: `vanavond` (this evening), `straks` (later today), `zo meteen` or just `zo` (in a moment), `morgen`, `overmorgen` (the day after tomorrow), `binnenkort` (soon), `volgende week`, `over twee dagen` (in two days: `over`, not `in`), `later`.

### 2. gaan + infinitive

`gaan` (ik ga, jij gaat, hij gaat, wij gaan) with an infinitive is the Dutch "going to". Use it for a **plan**, and for something that is **about to happen**: you can see it coming.

> Ik ga volgend jaar Spaans leren. — I am going to learn Spanish next year.
> Gaan jullie in de zomer weer kamperen? — Are you going camping again in the summer?
> Kijk naar die wolken: het gaat regenen. — Look at those clouds: it is going to rain.

Where it does not fit:

- Not with `gaan` itself: `Ik ga morgen naar de markt`, never *Ik ga morgen naar de markt gaan.
- With `komen` the present tense is normal: `Ik kom morgen`, rather than `Ik ga morgen komen`.
- With `zijn`, `hebben` and the modal verbs it is unusual. Use the present tense: `Morgen ben ik thuis`, `Ik heb morgen tijd`, `Ik moet morgen werken`.

### 3. zullen + infinitive

| | zullen |
| ik | zal |
| jij / je, u | zult / zal |
| hij, zij / ze, het | zal |
| wij / we, jullie, zij / ze | zullen |

`zullen` is not a neutral future. It always adds something:

- **a promise**: you give your word.
- **a proposal**, in a question with ik or we (unit A2 · 11).
- **a guess**, usually with `wel`: "probably".
- **a forecast** in formal or written Dutch, such as the weather report.

> Ik zal je morgen bellen. — I will call you tomorrow.
> Zullen we zondag gaan fietsen? — Shall we go cycling on Sunday?
> Het zal wel goed komen. — It will probably be all right.
> Morgen zal het in het hele land regenen. — Tomorrow it will rain in the whole country.

So `Ik zal morgen werken` is correct, but it sounds like a promise. For a plain fact about tomorrow say `Ik werk morgen`.

### Word order

`ga` or `zal` is the conjugated verb, so it stands where the verb always stands: second in a statement, first in a yes/no question. The infinitive goes to the **end**, as with the modal verbs. When a time word comes first, the subject follows the verb. A separable verb stays in one piece at the end.

> Morgen ga ik met mijn zus wandelen. — Tomorrow I am going for a walk with my sister.
> Ik zal een paraplu voor je meenemen. — I will bring an umbrella for you.

You will also hear a phrase with a preposition after the infinitive (`Ik ga wandelen in het bos`). For now, put the infinitive last.

### Watch out

- **No te.** English says "going *to* rain", Dutch does not: `Het gaat regenen`, never *Het gaat te regenen.
- **willen is not "will".** `Ik wil komen` means "I want to come". "I will come" is `Ik kom` or `Ik zal komen`.
- **Not gaan twice**: `Ik ga naar huis`, never *Ik ga naar huis gaan.
- **The infinitive goes last**: `Ik ga morgen een paraplu kopen`, not *Ik ga kopen morgen een paraplu.

### Compared with Ukrainian

Ukrainian builds a future with `буду` + infinitive: `Я буду працювати`. Do not turn every `буду` into `zal`. The normal Dutch is the present tense, `Ik werk morgen`, just as Ukrainian can say `Завтра я працюю`. In Dutch that is the rule, not the exception.

sentences.nl: Overmorgen gaan we naar het strand.
sentences.en: The day after tomorrow we are going to the beach.
sentences.note: The present tense with a time word is the normal future. Gaan is the main verb here (to go). Overmorgen stands first, so the verb comes before we.
alt: Overmorgen gaan wij naar het strand.

sentences.nl: Mijn ouders komen in de herfst naar Nederland.
sentences.en: My parents are coming to the Netherlands in the autumn.
sentences.note: With komen Dutch uses the present tense for the future, rather than gaan + komen. In de herfst shows that it is about later.
alt: In de herfst komen mijn ouders naar Nederland.

sentences.en: Later today the sun will shine again. (present tense)
sentences.note: Straks already says that it is about later, so the present tense is enough: schijnt. Straks stands first, so the subject de zon follows the verb.

sentences.nl: Mijn zus gaat in de lente trouwen.
sentences.en: My sister is going to get married in the spring.
sentences.note: gaan + infinitive for a plan. Gaat stands in second place and the infinitive trouwen goes to the end of the sentence.
alt: In de lente gaat mijn zus trouwen.

sentences.nl: Wat ga je dit weekend doen?
sentences.en: What are you going to do this weekend?
sentences.note: gaan + infinitive asks about a plan. It is jij gaat, but je directly after the verb loses the t: ga je. Doen stands at the end.
alt: Wat ga jij dit weekend doen?

sentences.en: It is going to rain in a moment.
sentences.note: gaan + infinitive for something that is about to happen: you can see the clouds. There is no te before regenen.

sentences.nl: Volgens het weerbericht gaat het morgen niet vriezen.
sentences.en: According to the weather forecast it is not going to freeze tomorrow.
sentences.note: Volgens het weerbericht is the first element, so gaat comes next and then the subject het. Niet stands before the infinitive at the end.

sentences.en: I will help you tomorrow. (a promise)
sentences.note: zullen for a promise: ik zal, without t. Not ik wil, which would mean 'I want to help you'. The infinitive helpen goes to the end.

sentences.nl: Zullen we morgen naar het bos gaan?
sentences.en: Shall we go to the forest tomorrow?
sentences.note: Zullen we …? is a proposal. Gaan is the infinitive here and stands at the end. With zullen that is fine; only gaan + gaan is impossible.
alt: Zullen wij morgen naar het bos gaan?

sentences.nl: Het zal morgen wel bewolkt zijn.
sentences.en: It will probably be cloudy tomorrow. (with zal … wel)
sentences.note: zal + wel is a guess: probably. With zijn Dutch uses zullen or the present tense (Het is morgen bewolkt) rather than gaan.
alt: Morgen zal het wel bewolkt zijn.

exercises.nl: Zie je die donkere wolken? We ___ nat worden.
exercises.en: Do you see those dark clouds? We are going to get wet.
exercises.note: We is plural, so gaan. This is gaan + infinitive for something you can see coming; the infinitive worden stands at the end.
After gaan the infinitive comes without te. English 'going to' has a 'to', but Dutch gaan takes the bare infinitive: gaan zwemmen.

exercises.nl: De temperatuur ___ morgen stijgen tot twintig graden.
exercises.en: Tomorrow the temperature will rise to twenty degrees.
exercises.note: A forecast in a weather report uses zullen, and de temperatuur is a third-person singular subject: zal. Wil means 'wants to', and zult goes with jij and u.

exercises.nl: Ik ___ morgen graag komen, maar ik kan niet.
exercises.en: I would like to come tomorrow, but I cannot.
exercises.note: willen says what you want, not what will happen. Zal would be a promise to come, and that does not go together with 'maar ik kan niet'.

exercises.nl: Wat ___ (gaan) je in de vakantie doen?
exercises.en: What are you going to do in the holidays?
exercises.note: It is jij gaat, but when je follows the verb the t disappears: ga je. The plan itself, doen, stands at the end as an infinitive.

exercises.en: We are going on holiday soon.
exercises.note: Here gaan is the main verb (to go) in the present tense, and binnenkort makes it future. A second gaan at the end is impossible: never 'wij gaan … gaan'.

exercises.nl: De bui ___ (zullen) zo wel voorbij zijn.
exercises.en: The shower will probably be over in a moment.
exercises.note: Hij, zij and het take zal, without t. Zal together with wel is a guess: probably.

exercises.nl: Over twee weken ___ (beginnen) het nieuwe seizoen.
exercises.en: The new season starts in two weeks.
exercises.note: The present tense is enough, because over twee weken already places it in the future. Het nieuwe seizoen is the subject: stem + t, begint.

answers: Straks ga ik een paraplu kopen.
exercises.en: Later today I am going to buy an umbrella.
exercises.note: Straks takes the first place, so ga comes second and ik follows it. The object stands before the infinitive, and the infinitive closes the sentence.

exercises.en: Shall I pick you up tomorrow?
exercises.note: An offer with Zal ik …? starts with the verb. The short pronoun je comes right after the subject, and the separable verb ophalen stays in one piece at the end.

exercises.en: Tomorrow it is not going to snow.
exercises.note: After Morgen comes the verb gaat, then the subject het. Niet stands before the infinitive at the end.

exercises.en: It is going to be very windy tomorrow.
exercises.note: Gaat takes the place of the conjugated verb, and waaien moves to the end as an infinitive, without te.

exercises.task: Write it the way a formal weather report does: with zullen.
exercises.note: Zal takes the second place and blijven goes to the end as an infinitive. In conversation the present tense, Morgen blijft het droog, is more usual.

exercises.task: Say it the everyday way: in the present tense, without zullen.
exercises.from: Wij zullen volgende week niet thuis zijn.
answers: Wij zijn volgende week niet thuis.
We zijn volgende week niet thuis.
exercises.en: We are not at home next week.
exercises.note: Volgende week already shows that it is about the future, so the present tense of zijn is enough. With zijn this is the normal choice.

exercises.wrong: Ik ga morgen naar de markt gaan.
answers: Ik ga morgen naar de markt.
Ik zal morgen naar de markt gaan.
exercises.en: I am going to the market tomorrow.
exercises.note: gaan + infinitive is not used with gaan itself. The present tense of gaan together with morgen is enough. (With zal it would be a promise.)

exercises.wrong: Morgen wil het de hele dag regenen.
answers: Morgen zal het de hele dag regenen.
Morgen gaat het de hele dag regenen.
Morgen regent het de hele dag.
exercises.en: Tomorrow it will rain all day.
exercises.note: willen means 'to want', and the weather does not want anything. English 'will' is zullen, gaan or simply the present tense.
